:::: section
## The tools, in plain English

::: tool-grid
### Conda: sets up the workspace

Think of Conda as setting up a classroom before a lesson. It gives us
Python and larger tools such as Quarto and Jupyter. The shopping list is
`environment.yml`.

### Poetry: keeps the Python list

Poetry installs Python add-ons and records their versions.
`pyproject.toml` describes the project; `poetry.lock` records the exact
versions chosen.

### Jupyter: the exercise book

A notebook mixes notes and Python code cells. We saved ours as
`notebooks/tooling-lab.ipynb`.

### Quarto: the publisher

Quarto takes the notebook and makes an HTML page from it. When asked, it
also runs the notebook cells through Python.

### Makim: the task organiser

Makim reads `.makim.yaml` and gives commands short, memorable names. It
starts the right tool for each task.

### Git: the project history book

Git records the files and changes, so we can keep the working Stage 1
setup as a checkpoint before trying Stage 2.
:::
::::

::: section
## What happens when we render?

First, we name the job: `lab.render`. Makim looks up that job in
`.makim.yaml`, then starts the command written there. Quarto uses Python
and Jupyter to run the notebook cells and makes the finished HTML
lesson.

One more Nigerian picture: Conda sets up the market stall with the main
tools, and Poetry keeps the written list of Python add-ons and versions.
Makim is the park marshal; it sends the job to Quarto, but it does not
drive the danfo or run the notebook code itself.

The full command saved in Makim is:

    quarto render notebooks/tooling-lab.ipynb --to html --execute

We type a task name instead of remembering that whole command. The
`--execute` part tells Quarto to run the notebook cells while rendering.
Without it, Quarto expects the notebook to have already been run and
saved.

::: section
## Problems we hit and how we fixed them

We built the setup one step at a time. These problems helped us learn
which tool was responsible and what it needed.

1.  **The folder was empty and was not a Git repo.** Git could not show
    a branch or remote yet. We cloned the GitHub repo into the folder,
    then created the Stage 1 branch.
2.  **Conda was not found after installation.** We chose not to let the
    installer edit the shell profile. We loaded Conda\'s shell hook in
    the current terminal; a new terminal needs the hook again unless we
    choose to initialize the shell later.
3.  **Poetry saw Python 3.13 instead of the required 3.12.** The old
    `VIRTUAL_ENV` setting pointed at another virtual environment. We
    used `env -u VIRTUAL_ENV` for the Poetry command so it could use the
    Conda Python 3.12 environment.
4.  **There were no project setup files to start from.** We wrote
    `environment.yml`, `pyproject.toml` and `.makim.yaml` ourselves in
    Neovim. That made each file\'s purpose visible instead of hiding it
    behind a setup wizard.
5.  **Poetry refreshed packages already in the Conda environment.** The
    install showed many package updates. It completed successfully, but
    it also showed that Poetry and Conda were working in the same
    environment during this experiment.
6.  **Makim first stopped with "No module named click".** Makim needed
    the Python package `click`, but it was missing from the project\'s
    install. We added it to `pyproject.toml`, refreshed the lock file,
    and installed again.
7.  **Makim first said its config file was missing.** It looks for
    `.makim.yaml` by default. We created that file and added the
    `lab.hello` and `lab.render` tasks.
8.  **YAML treated punctuation in a command as special syntax.** We
    quoted the full `echo` command in the YAML file so its colon was
    read as part of the text.
9.  **`quarto update` asked us for an extension.** That command is for
    updating a Quarto extension, not a general software updater. We used
    Quarto\'s version and render commands for this lab instead.
10. **Our first search did not find the notebook\'s greeting.** The code
    had not yet been saved in the notebook file. We saved the notebook
    and checked `tooling-lab.ipynb` again.
11. **The first HTML page did not show fresh cell output.** Quarto had
    not been told to execute the notebook. Adding `--execute` made it
    run the cells before writing HTML.
12. **Generated files appeared as untracked Git files.** Jupyter
    checkpoints and Quarto\'s HTML and supporting files are build
    output. We added ignore rules so they do not clutter normal Git
    status.
13. **Xonsh printed a deprecation warning.** Makim selected Xonsh as its
    shell and one old setting was deprecated. The warning did not stop
    either task; both Makim commands completed.
:::

::: section
## What difference did Makim make?

Without Makim, we would type the long Quarto command ourselves. With
Makim, the command has a name: `lab.render`. The task is written down
once, so we can run it again later or share it with another learner.

### Makim helps with repeatable tasks

- Run the notebook or build course pages.
- Run checks and tests before sharing changes.
- Format or check code with tools such as Ruff.
- Preview lessons or documentation on a laptop.
- Clean generated files when we want a fresh build.

Those are ideas for future tasks. In Stage 1, we made `lab.hello` and
`lab.render`.
:::

::: section
## The full Makim file, explained line by line

This is the whole `.makim.yaml` file we made. It gives two commands
short names.

    groups:
      lab:
        tasks:
          hello:
            help: Confirm Makim runs in Stage 1
            run: 'echo "Stage 1: Conda + Poetry + Makim"'
          render:
            help: Render the Jupyter notebook to HTML with Quarto
            run: quarto render notebooks/tooling-lab.ipynb --to html --execute

1.  `groups:` tells Makim that task groups follow.
2.  `lab:` names our group. It becomes the first part of a task name.
3.  `tasks:` starts the list of commands Makim can run.
4.  `hello:` names the first task. Together, the group and task make
    `lab.hello`.
5.  `help:` is the short explanation shown in Makim\'s help screen.
6.  `run:` tells Makim what shell command to run. Here, `echo` prints a
    message.
7.  `render:` names the second task. Together with `lab`, it becomes
    `lab.render`.
8.  The second `help:` describes the render task in the help screen.
9.  The second `run:` starts Quarto. `render` means make an output file;
    the notebook path is the input; `--to html` chooses a web page;
    `--execute` tells Quarto to run the Python cells first.

### The command we typed

    env -u VIRTUAL_ENV poetry run makim lab.render

- `env -u VIRTUAL_ENV` hides the old Python environment setting for this
  one command.
- `poetry run` starts the next command in the environment Poetry is
  using.
- `makim` starts the task runner.
- `lab.render` asks it to run the `render` task in the `lab` group.

The full command is used because this computer had an old environment
setting pointing to Python 3.13. In this Stage 1 setup, removing that
setting lets Poetry use the Conda environment with Python 3.12.
:::

::: section
## What Makim does not do

Makim does not install Python, manage package versions, or write
notebook lessons. Conda and Poetry set up the tools and packages.
Jupyter runs code cells. Quarto renders the notebook. Makim coordinates
the commands.

The notebook is stored on GitHub, and the link above opens it in Google
Colab. The rendered HTML file is a separate web page.
:::

::: section
## What comes next?

Stage 1 is our saved starting point: Conda + Poetry + Makim. Next, we

:::

## The QMD-first setup we use now

The earlier sections and diagrams describe our first version. We now keep two QMD source files:

- `stage-1-guide.qmd` is the blog page. Makim task `lab.guide` asks Quarto to create `stage-1-guide.html`.
- `notebooks/tooling-lab.qmd` is the notebook source. Makim task `lab.notebook` asks Quarto to create `notebooks/tooling-lab.ipynb`.

The guide and the notebook both link to the same Colab notebook. The notebook can also be downloaded from the guide. `quarto convert` creates the notebook file; it does not run its Python code. Open the notebook in Colab to run the code there.

Makim is like the marshal at a Lagos motor park: it sends each job to the right place. Quarto does the document work, and Colab is where the learner runs the notebook.

The two Makim tasks are:

```yaml
notebook:
  run: quarto convert notebooks/tooling-lab.qmd --output notebooks/tooling-lab.ipynb
guide:
  run: quarto render stage-1-guide.qmd --to html
```

Run them with:

```text
env -u VIRTUAL_ENV poetry run makim lab.notebook
env -u VIRTUAL_ENV poetry run makim lab.guide
```

Learn more: [Makim documentation](https://makim.org/) · [Quarto and
Python notebooks](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/python)
